lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: What’s this, Alexander? You’re dead too, like the rest of us?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: You can see that, Diogenes. Hardly surprising, if a man dies.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: So Ammon was lying when he said you were his son. You were Philip’s after all.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Philip’s, obviously. If I had been Ammon’s, I wouldn’t be dead.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And yet they said the same sort of thing about Olympias: a snake was visiting her, seen in her bed, and that was how you were born—while Philip was being fooled, thinking you were his.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I heard all that too, same as you. Now I see there wasn’t a sound word in anything my mother or Ammon’s prophets said.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Still, their lie wasn’t useless to you, Alexander. A great many people cowered because they thought you were a god.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But tell me—who did you leave that enormous empire to?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I don’t know, Diogenes. I didn’t live long enough to give instructions about it—except that, as I was dying, I handed Perdiccas my ring. But why are you laughing?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Why else? I was remembering what Greece did when you had just inherited the throne: flattering you, choosing you as protector and general against the barbarians; some even adding you to the twelve gods, building you temples, and sacrificing to you as the son of a snake.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But tell me—where did the Macedonians bury you?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I’m still lying in Babylon. This is the thirtieth day. Ptolemy, my bodyguard, promises that, if he ever gets a free moment from the troubles under his feet, he’ll carry me off to Egypt and bury me there, so I can become one of the Egyptian gods.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And I’m not supposed to laugh, Alexander, when I see you still talking nonsense even in Hades, still hoping to become Anubis or Osiris? No, my very divine friend—don’t pin hopes on that. Once a man has crossed the lake and come inside the mouth of this place, it is not permitted to go back up. Aeacus is not negligent, and Cerberus is not exactly easy to ignore.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: There is one thing I’d be glad to learn from you: how do you bear it when you remember how much happiness you left behind above ground—bodyguards, shield-bearers, satraps, all that gold, nations bowing down, Babylon, Bactra, the great elephants, the honour, the glory, the spectacle of riding out in state with a white ribbon round your head and a purple cloak pinned at your shoulder. Doesn’t it hurt when all that comes back to mind? Why are you crying, you poor fool? Didn’t wise Aristotle even teach you this much—not to think the gifts of fortune are permanent?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Wise? That man was the most polished flatterer of them all. Let me tell you what Aristotle was, since I knew him: what he asked from me, the sort of letters he wrote, the way he exploited my vanity about education—soft-soaping me, praising me one moment for my beauty, as if beauty too were part of the Good, and the next for my achievements and my wealth. Wealth, yes: he held that to be a good as well, so he wouldn’t have to be ashamed of taking it himself. A charlatan, Diogenes. A professional. Still, I have at least profited from his wisdom in one respect: I grieve as if those things you listed just now really were the greatest goods.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Then do you know what you should do? I’ll prescribe you a cure for grief. Since hellebore doesn’t grow down here, go take a deep, open-mouthed drink of Lethe-water. Then drink again. And again. That way you’ll stop tormenting yourself over Aristotle’s ‘goods.’ Besides, I can see Cleitus over there, and Callisthenes, and plenty of others, all coming straight for you, eager to tear you apart and pay you back for what you did to them. So take that other road there, and drink often, as I said.
